headline: ByteDance gained access to over 2,000 Nvidia B200 chips through Norway data center
summary: China's ByteDance secured 2,304 Nvidia B200 chips via a Norwegian data center deal, exploiting U.S. export control loopholes. This arrangement exposes the company to regulatory and reputational risks.
details: UK-based "neocloud" Nscale built its business on a major deal with Spring, a Singaporean subsidiary of ByteDance. This contract, accounting for $24 million of Nscale's 2025 revenue, granted Spring access to 2,304 Nvidia B200 chips at Nscale's Glomfjord, Norway, data center.

The arrangement came to light through Nscale's S-1 documents filed for an initial public offering in the U.S. While ByteDance or its subsidiary weren't directly named in the S-1, a supporting $105 million loan agreement with Macquarie identified Spring (SG) Pte Ltd as a significant customer.

A month after drawing the first loan tranche, Nscale secured deals with Microsoft and Nvidia, with Jensen Huang committing over $660 million. Nvidia has since increased its commitments to over $2 billion, plus an additional $860 million guarantee on Nscale's Texas facility lease.

This funding and Nvidia's commitments helped Nscale secure larger deals, including a $44 billion contract with Microsoft and a $45 billion deal with Anthropic. Nscale expects its Spring contract to fall below 20% of its overall revenue and shrink further with new Western clients.

Due to Spring's link to ByteDance, Macquarie mandated Nscale to monitor the Chinese subsidiary's use of AI chips and report any "compute anomalies or suspicious configurations" that might violate U.S. export controls. A third party also conducted due diligence on ByteDance and Spring to ensure legal compliance.

Chinese companies have been exploiting loopholes in U.S. export controls to access advanced AI chips, often by renting them from foreign companies or using overseas subsidiaries for direct purchases. The U.S. has recently moved to close these loopholes, though it's unclear how this will impact the existing Spring-Nscale deal.

headline_marked: Alibaba unveils Zhenwu V900, claims [[most powerful AI chip in China]]
headline: Alibaba unveils Zhenwu V900, claims most powerful AI chip in China
summary: Alibaba's new Zhenwu V900 AI accelerator boasts three times the performance of its predecessor and is designed to support massive future AI models. It's slated for mass production in early 2027.
details: Alibaba has announced its new Zhenwu V900 AI accelerator, with CEO Eddie Wu claiming it is the most powerful AI chip in China. This new chip is designed to support the training of future Qwen models with parameter counts ranging from 5 to 10 trillion, a significant leap from current models.

The Zhenwu V900 is an AI training and inference processor featuring 216 GB of GPU memory and 1,200 GB/s of inter-chip bandwidth. It can scale out to clusters of up to 500,000 cards, promising substantial performance gains over the previous generation M890 chip.

Mass production and commercial release of the Zhenwu V900 are scheduled for the first quarter of 2027, an accelerated timeline compared to previous company roadmaps. Alibaba has already shipped over 650,000 Zhenwu chips to external customers, with an annual refresh cycle planned.

While specific technical details like FLOPS or process node are not yet disclosed, the V900 offers significant improvements in memory capacity and inter-chip bandwidth compared to the M890. The company aims to achieve data center capacity of over 20 gigawatts by 2032, though supply chain shortages pose a challenge.

In parallel, Alibaba is advancing its Qwen model family, with Qwen 4 currently in training and future versions 4.5 and 5 planned to scale even further. The company also reported significant improvements in chip-design experiments using its AI tools, achieving area cuts without performance loss.
